definition: Promulgate means to formally and officially proclaim a law or rule to the public.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word promulgate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know promulgate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Universities promulgate their honor codes loudly during orientation week, printing them in every handbook and reading them aloud at convocation.
To post a notice is the minimum gesture — one sheet on one board; it stops far short of promulgate.
Announce goes further than post, actively telling an audience, but promulgate crowns the ladder: a formal, official proclamation pushed out until the whole public is presumed to know.

To proclaim is to announce something publicly and grandly — from a balcony, in banner type. Promulgate adds legal machinery to the moment: an authority formally puts a law or rule on the record before the public. A love of trumpets is enough to proclaim; only office lets you promulgate.

To decree is to command by authority: the ruling itself, the order that something now be so. To promulgate is to spread the official word of a law or rule until the public is presumed to know it. A decree commands; promulgation broadcasts what was commanded.

The pro- ('out, forward') is plain enough, but Romans left no clear record of what -mulgare meant: one guess connects it to vulgus, 'the common people,' another to mulgere, 'to milk out.' With the root's identity disputed, English has no safe relative to point to.
Promulgate means to formally and officially proclaim a law or rule to the public.

When the island nation adopted its first constitution, criers promulgated it the old way: read in full from every church step, printed on broadsheets, nailed to the harbor board — so that no fisherman could later claim the law was a secret.
Promulgate is official and outward-facing: an authority formally proclaims a law, doctrine or policy and puts it before the public.
Announcing tells; promulgating tells with authority and on the record, which is why constitutions are promulgated while parties are merely announced.
Promulgate belongs to governments, courts and churches: laws, doctrines and regulations are promulgated.
For everyday news, announce; for informal spreading, circulate — a word in this unit's reference list.
If no authority stands behind the message, promulgate will sound comically grand.
